_comment: RULES THAT REQUIRE MANUAL REPETITION, and whether they have ever actually run. The owner's framing: a rule the tooling makes impractical is not a rule in force, and documentation claiming it IS in force is a false claim about our own process — the same family as the badge claim. Every verdict below has evidence beside it; where the evidence is weak, the verdict says so.

rules.rule: Run gate-check.mjs over EVERY batch file before any release, not only when a batch is first written.
rules.howIKnow: The script took `process.argv[2]` — a single path. Executing the rule meant 45 hand invocations. Running it across the dataset for the first time immediately found 2 entry-video titles renamed at the source and 1 outgrown size band, which would not have survived a single prior full run.
rules.fix: gate-check.mjs --all. 328 entry videos, 240 units, now 0 failures.

rules.rule: Contrast is verified by script: 22 pairings across both themes, all passing WCAG AA. Re-run after any palette change.
rules.verdict: NEVER RUN — THE SCRIPT DID NOT EXIST
rules.howIKnow: No file matching contrast/a11y/color appears anywhere in `git log --all --name-only`. It was never added and never deleted; it was never there.
rules.fix: scripts/check-contrast.mjs written and run. The claim's substance held — 0 failures — but the count was wrong: 30 pairings, not 22. The corrected sentence names the script.
rules.note: The worst of this class. An inward-facing claim about our own rigour, carrying a specific measured number, produced by nothing.

rules.rule: MARKUP.md is the DOM contract. Markup change and MARKUP.md change go in the same commit.
rules.howIKnow: Of the 16 most recent commits touching js/ or index.html, 2 also touched MARKUP.md. The rule is real and cheap; it is simply not being done, including by me — the `dormant` meta label added this batch changed rendered markup and did not update MARKUP.md.
rules.fix: NOT FIXED. A commit-time check would need a hook, and whether a js change is a markup change cannot be decided mechanically. Recorded as a known gap rather than closed.

rules.howIKnow: It read '200 categories, each with 5+ creators' and '700 verified unique creators' while the live targets are 197 categories at depth 2 and a 400-creator cap. It also said validate.mjs 'passes on the current empty dataset' with 233 creators in it.
rules.fix: Updated, with the old numbers left visible so the drift is legible rather than erased.

rules.rule: Commit after every batch and every phase.
rules.howIKnow: Every batch file in data/creators has a corresponding commit; git log shows one commit per batch with the batch named in the subject.

rules.rule: Run the gate over the finished batch file; zero failures is the bar for committing.
rules.howIKnow: Distinct from the 'every batch file' rule above, and this one only needs one invocation per batch. Each batch's report records the gate result. It is the per-batch version that ran; the whole-dataset version that never did.

rules.rule: Keep the Netlify form name attributes in sync between index.html and formMarkup().
rules.howIKnow: index.html declares form-name, bot-field, source, note and the form name `how-did-you-hear`; js/components/how-did-you-hear.js sets FORM_NAME to the same string and formMarkup emits the same four names. Checked directly.
Both written this batch. Named here so that a later audit can ask the same question of them, since a rule added today is the most likely to be assumed rather than checked.

_whatThisClassLooksLike: In all four failures the documentation asserted a procedure was in force. Nothing lied about the data; the claim was about US. The distinguishing test is not 'is this rule good' but 'can one command execute it, and is there evidence it ran'. A rule that needs N manual repetitions will be executed zero times.
